newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end slightly lower, bracing for CPI.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end slightly lower, bracing for CPI.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended slightly lower on Monday, as fears of a strong consumer inflation report kept the market under pressure.
Trading activity, though, was extremely light, with most retail accounts opting to stay on the sidelines ahead of Tuesday's consumer price report.
"It's been a painful day," said Scott Graham, trader at Prudential Securities Inc, referring to the lack of action.
Underscoring that sentiment was bond prices sticking to a 5/32 range, while two-year notes traded in a 2/32 range.
Late Monday, the 30-year bond was at 93-10/32, down 1/32, to yield 7.17 percent. The two-year note was down 2/32 at 99-16/32 to yield 6.52 percent.
With no key economic data or comments from Federal Reserve officials on Monday, market participants set their sights on the all-important CPI report, due Tuesday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Overall CPI is expected to have risen 0.2 percent, with the "core" rate seen up 0.3 percent in March, according to a Reuters poll.
Yet, the market fears stronger numbers, traders said.

Pat Alexander, head trader at BankAmerica Securities Inc, said the surprisingly robust 0.4 percent jump in the March core producer price index intensified market fears that the core CPI will also be strong.

"If the core CPI is disroportionatley strong, the market will say ... the Fed is possibly behind the curve instead of being pre-emptive," he said. A strong report "would be hard evidence of inflation possibly beginning to build and not just some fear on the part of the Central Bank."
He described Monday as a "day of expectations." Tuesday, he added, "will be more of a day of reality."

A 0.3 percent rise in the core is priced in, but a reading of 0.4 percent or above would likely spark a selloff, traders said. Treasuries could rally on a weaker-than-expected CPI, such as a 0.2 percent core increase, players said. But some argued that any rally would be short-lived, citing continuing expectations of a 25-basis-point rate hike at the May 20 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.
"The market is trading like a bear market; in a bear market you trade off into economic data," Graham said. "The market ... still has to work out when economic strength is going to slow."
In anticipation of a strong CPI, many Treasury market participants took Monday off, leaving dealers to mainly square positions.

Only the bill sector stayed above water, but bill traders said the market was supported early by the large decline in stock prices. Once the stock market recovered in the afternoon, bills came under a bit of pressure, traders noted.
Helping to boost bills was a successful weekly auction, in which the Treasury sold $12 billion three- and six-month bills at rates of 5.15 percent and 5.42 percent respectively.
The when-issued three-month bill ended the day at 5.16 percent, while the when-issued six-month bill was at 5.435 percent. The outstanding year-bill was at 5.68 percent.
The 10-year note closed down 2/32 at 94-28/32, yielding 6.98 percent. The five-year note traded off 2/32 at 99-1/32 to yield 6.86 percent.
According to GovPX, trading volume on Monday was $65 billion.
Also of interest on Tuesday, February business inventories are due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, while Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi and Redbook Research will release weekly chain store and retail sales data.
